title: Status pages and the trust around them
metaTitle: Status pages that keep trust intact
excerpt: During an incident the status page is the product. Say what is affected, what you know, and when you will update. Leave the decoration for a calmer day.
alt: An open notebook with the word Notes underlined, a fountain pen, and glasses on a wooden desk, the tools of a plain update for an article about status pages.
caption: A notebook ready for the next plain update. Photograph via Unsplash.

faqs.question: What should a status update include?
faqs.answer: Say what is affected, what you know so far, and when the next update will come. Use words a customer uses for the feature, not only an internal service name. If you do not know the cause yet, say that you do not know, and keep the time of the next note.

faqs.question: Should status rely on color?
faqs.answer: Color can support a state, and it cannot be the only signal. Pair it with a word such as disrupted, degraded, or operational. People who cannot distinguish the color, and people reading a text-only paste in a chat, still need the meaning.

faqs.question: Where should the status page be linked during an incident?
faqs.answer: Link it from the product, from the docs, and from the message you send while people are stuck. A footer link they must remember is not a plan. The page should load even when the app does not, which means it should not live only inside the broken system.

markdown:
Status page design matters most on the day something is broken. In that hour the status page is the product. People are not browsing your brand. They are deciding whether you know, whether their work is affected, and when you will speak again.

Say those three things, in that order. What is affected. What you know. When the next update will be. Decoration can wait for a day when nobody is stuck.

## The page has one job during an incident

Open with the current state in a sentence a customer can paste into their own team chat. "Exports are failing for workspaces in the EU. We are investigating. Next update by 14:10 UTC." That sentence is the product. A hero illustration of a cloud is not.

Name the feature in the customer's language. "The billing service" may be accurate inside your architecture and meaningless to the person who cannot download an invoice. If several features share a cause, list the features. Readers should not have to infer their own impact from a codename.

[Google's people-first guidance](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) asks for content with a real purpose, from a source a reader can identify. A status page's purpose is the incident. Sign it. The company name, and a way to know the page is official. An unsigned widget on a third-party domain, with no link from your product, will be doubted at the exact moment you need to be believed.

Put the time on every update, including the timezone. "Soon" is not a time. A clock you miss is a trust problem, so set a time you can keep, and update again even if the news is "we are still investigating." Silence reads as absence. A repeated note reads as attention.

## What you know, and what you do not

Separate observation from theory. "Invoices created after 09:00 are missing the tax line" is an observation. "We think a deploy caused it" is a theory, and it should be labeled as such, or held until you are sure. Customers make decisions on your sentences. A guessed cause that you retract an hour later costs more than a plain "we do not know the cause yet."

Say who is affected when you know. All customers. Only accounts created this week. Only the mobile app. Partial impact stated clearly is more trustworthy than a green banner with a quiet exception in paragraph four. If you are not sure of the boundary, say the boundary is still being checked, and name what you have confirmed.

Avoid blame as a pastime. A vendor, a cloud region, a bug you are ashamed of: the customer needs the effect and the next note. The postmortem can carry the cause when people are no longer blocked. During the incident, a paragraph about how seriously you take reliability is time you could have spent on the sentence they came for.

Keep a history on the page. Newest update first, older ones still readable. People arrive mid-incident and need the latest line. People who were here at the start need to see that you have not contradicted yourself without a trace. Deleting the early notes to look tidy looks like a cover. Leave them. Add a line when a fact changes.

## Color is a hint, not the message

Red, amber, and green are a convention, not a sentence. [The W3C's WCAG overview](https://www.w3.org/WAI/standards-guidelines/wcag/) is the public reference for not relying on color alone to convey meaning. A status dot with no word fails that test, and it fails the paste test too. Someone will screenshot the page into a chat or copy a line into a ticket. The word has to travel without the pixel.

Use a small set of words and define them once, in plain language. Operational means the feature is working as offered. Degraded means it works with a limitation you describe. Disrupted means the job cannot be finished. Maintenance means you planned this window. Do not invent a new adjective per incident. The vocabulary is part of the trust.

Do not paint the whole page red as a brand moment. Contrast still has to hold for the body text. A status page that looks like a poster will be hard to read for the person who needs it most, on a phone, in a bright room, while their own customer is waiting. Type, size, and a single column will do more than a status illustration.

If you show a component list, each row needs a word, not only a pill of color. Sort the disrupted rows to the top during an incident. A long alphabetical list that hides the broken feature under M is a design that has forgotten why the page exists.

## Where people must be able to find it

The page has to load when the app does not. Host it so a failure in the product does not take the explanation with it. Link it from the product's error state, from the login screen if login is what failed, and from the docs. Teach the empty and error states to point here when the cause is an outage rather than a user mistake.

Your own team needs the link in the first reply they send. A support macro that says "we are looking" without the URL creates a second channel of rumors. The status page should be the channel. Social posts can point at it. They should not be a divergent story with a different ETA.

Write the URL so it is easy to say on a call. A short path on your domain beats a long link on a status vendor if you can keep the reliability promise. If you use a vendor, still put a link on your domain that redirects, so the address you print does not change when the tool does. Test the redirect before you need it.

During a quiet month, the page should still look alive. A history of recent days, mostly operational, is reassuring. A blank page, or a page that has not been touched in a year, suggests you do not have a habit. The habit is the product. The incident is when the habit becomes visible.

## The cadence of updates

Pick a cadence at the start of the incident and keep it. Every thirty minutes for a full disruption. Every hour if the impact is narrow and stable. Say the cadence in the first note. If you need to slow down, say why: "we are in a change window and the next note will be at 16:00." Vanishing between notes is how a correct fix still feels chaotic.

The person writing the notes should not be the only person debugging, if you can help it. Writing is a job. It requires the facts, and it requires sentences. One engineer talking to the note-taker is faster than asking the person in the logs to also be eloquent. On a small team the same person may do both. Even then, draft the sentence before you return to the terminal, so the update does not slip.

Templates help if they are short. Affected. Known. Next update. Impact if people must act. A template that includes an apology paragraph and a values statement will be skipped, or worse, sent instead of the facts. Keep the template boring. Boring is the tone you want when money or data is in question.

After resolution, one note that says what is restored, what might still be cached or delayed, and whether any action is required. Then stop. A second essay at midnight helps the writer more than the reader. The changelog can record the repair the next day, in calmer language, with a link back for anyone who wants the trail.

## What not to decorate

Do not illustrate the outage. A sad robot, a burning data center, a joke. The reader is not in a mood to admire the craft. They are late. Humor that lands in the office will not land in their customer's meeting. Plain sentences are the courtesy.

Do not upsell. A status page with a newsletter modal, a request to follow you, or a banner for a new plan is a page that has forgotten itself. [Helpful content](https://developers.google.com/search/docs/fundamentals/creating-helpful-content) is a fair test: would this page still be respectful if the reader is having a bad day because of you. Take the modal off. Leave the facts.

Do not hide partial degradation to protect a graph. A public uptime number that stays at a perfect figure while exports are broken will be screenshotted next to the complaints. If you publish a number, define it, and let the incident move it. If you cannot define it, do not publish it. A truthful sentence beats a precise-looking percentage you will have to walk back.

Do not require a login to read status. The people who need it may be the people who cannot log in. Public page. No account wall. If you must share a more sensitive postmortem later, that document can be gated. The live notes cannot.

## After the incident, keep the habit

Hold a short review. Did the first note land while the impact was still being discovered. Was the cadence kept. Did the words match the features customers named in tickets. Write the answers where the next incident owner will see them. A status page without a ritual becomes a login nobody remembers.

Update the error states in the product if they pointed nowhere, or pointed at a generic contact form. The link to status should be conditional on a real incident if you can manage that, so ordinary validation errors do not send people to an all-clear page and confuse them. When there is no incident, the error should say what the user can fix. When there is one, the error can add the status line.

Decide what "all clear" requires. The feature works. The backlog of delayed jobs has drained, if that matters. The note says so. Then leave the history in place. People will check back. Let them see a closed story.

Empty states and errors are the other half of this trust, on ordinary days when nothing is on fire. [Empty states that sell the next step](/blog/empty-states-that-sell-the-next-step) is about the first screen inside the product, which should be as plain and as specific as a good status note. Read it when the incident page is in good shape and the day-to-day screens still shrug.

If you want to see how a public product surface stays specific under stress and in ordinary use, look at [Hanabi's selected work](https://tryhanabi.com/#works). The relevant question is whether a stranger can tell what is going on without a narrator.
